metadata.notes: Original-source research confirmed dated weather events, with station-observation time-window caveats. Deliberately deferred 7 stories whose date/hazard overlaps existing primaries.

reviews.title_after: A Washington blizzard forces Taft's inauguration indoors
reviews.core_fact: A severe snowstorm and gusty winds on March 4, 1909 forced William Howard Taft's inauguration ceremony into the Senate Chamber in Washington, D.C.
reviews.source_dependence: The U.S. Senate ceremonial history and NWS Washington's archival weather account separately corroborate the exact March 4 date, city and indoor ceremony, although their snow/cleanup figures may share archival Weather Bureau and Congressional records.
reviews.unverified_cautions: The blizzard began March 3 and lasted into March 4; NWS rounds snow accumulation to 10 inches while an archival Weather Bureau figure is 9.8 inches. Do not reuse Library of Congress photographs without item-level rights checks.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original March 4 inauguration route and synoptic snow/wind map comparing official weather observations.

reviews.title_after: Cyclone Remal begins crossing the Bangladesh–India coast
reviews.location_after: Coastal Bangladesh and West Bengal, India
reviews.core_fact: On May 26, 2024, Severe Cyclonic Storm Remal began crossing the coasts of Bangladesh and adjoining India's West Bengal state, with damaging wind, rain and coastal inundation risk.
reviews.source_dependence: IMD's May 26 operational cyclone bulletin documents proximity, track and projected coast crossing; the retrospective ACAPS and UN summaries independently assign landfall to May 26. IMD cyclone intensity estimates are cited downstream rather than independently measured by humanitarian analysts.
reviews.unverified_cautions: A cyclone's landfall begins and ends over several hours, straddling the May 26–27 calendar boundary in different bulletins. Do not confuse forecast storm surge heights with observed inundation or give the May 27 death toll as a May 26 impact count.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original Sundarbans coast map with May 26 satellite track and UTC, BST and IST time labels.

reviews.title_after: The Brazos River reaches a historic flood crest near Richmond, Texas
reviews.location_after: Richmond and Fort Bend County, Texas
reviews.core_fact: By June 2, 2016 the Brazos River near Richmond had reached a historic flood crest following torrential late-May rain in southeast Texas, inundating communities in Fort Bend County.
reviews.source_dependence: USGS provides June 2 Landsat-era flood context and ABC News independently reports the Richmond gauge record crest on June 2; the exact river measurement itself derives from a common NWS/USGS hydrologic gauge network.
reviews.unverified_cautions: A Richmond gauge crest is not the same as crests near Rosharon or West Columbia, which occurred on different days. Reported approximately 55-foot height is site-and-datum-specific. The original Cold Spring NCEI report is not this Brazos River event.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original May 26–June 2 rain accumulation map and Richmond gauge-stage hydrograph with station datum.

reviews.title_before: Flash Flood — SOUTH PORTION, North Carolina
reviews.title_after: Tropical Storm Bill makes landfall on Matagorda Island
reviews.core_fact: Tropical Storm Bill made landfall on Matagorda Island, Texas, on June 16, 2015 at about 11:45 a.m. CDT, bringing coastal winds and rain before the system moved inland.
reviews.source_dependence: NHC post-storm best-track analysis, the NWS Lake Charles local retrospective and NASA GPM satellite imagery agree on June 16 Texas landfall; NHC and NWS use shared recon and coastal observation inputs.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Do not confuse Bill's landfall with its later inland heavy-rain/flood impacts or use NASA's display of 11:45 a.m. CST as a daylight-saving-correct timestamp; June 16 Texas local civil time is CDT. Wind is tropical-storm intensity, not hurricane intensity.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original Matagorda Island satellite track and GPM precipitation-rate swath with UTC/CDT label.

reviews.title_after: A giant haboob swallows the Phoenix metropolitan area
reviews.core_fact: During the evening of July 5, 2011, an enormous thunderstorm-outflow dust wall swept across Phoenix, sharply reducing visibility and briefly closing Sky Harbor airport.
reviews.source_dependence: NWS Phoenix radar, warnings and trained reports date and explain the convective outflow; NASA Earth Observatory independently documents the visible dust wall and airport impact but relies partly on contemporary media meteorological reports.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Storm arrival evening July 5 MST is early July 6 UTC. NASA satellite imagery showing lingering dust was captured July 6, not at the height of July 5 haboob; treat 'mile high' or '100 miles wide' as estimates.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original modeled cold pool/outflow and visibility map with Phoenix 2011 local warning times.

reviews.title_after: Mumbai's extraordinary monsoon deluge overwhelms drainage
reviews.secondary_publisher: The Indian Express, referencing IMD station records
reviews.core_fact: Exceptional monsoon rainfall struck Mumbai on July 26, 2005; the Santacruz observing site recorded roughly 940–945 mm in a 24-hour period ending the following morning, associated with catastrophic flooding.
reviews.source_dependence: NASA's TRMM overpass on July 26 illustrates the rainfall concentration and the Indian Express independently recounts IMD Santacruz station history; the 24-hour gauge figure has a common underlying IMD observation.
reviews.unverified_cautions: NASA gives a rounded 942 mm versus IMD-derived 944.2 mm. The 24-hour observing window ended on July 27; do not imply 944.2 mm was measured only between 00 and 24 local July 26. NASA's satellite rainfall image is not automatically public-domain if partner marks additional rights.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original localized monsoon rain cell and Santacruz/Colaba side-by-side 24-hour gauge comparison.

reviews.title_after: A 1.67-pound hailstone falls in Coffeyville, Kansas
reviews.core_fact: On September 3, 1970, a giant hailstone fell at Coffeyville, Kansas, later documented as weighing 1.67 pounds and measuring 17.5 inches in circumference.
reviews.source_dependence: The City's dated archived artifact description and NWS historical summary corroborate the date and measured weight; both likely reproduce the same original hailstone measurement from the specimen, not independent weighings.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Coffeyville's 1970 hailstone held a historic heaviest-stone distinction; avoid claiming it still holds every largest- or heaviest-hail record worldwide. Stone weight, diameter and circumference are not interchangeable measurements.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original hailstone-scale graphic with diameter, circumference, mass, and updraft conceptual sketch.

reviews.title_after: Storm Daniel begins a historic Mediterranean rain disaster
reviews.core_fact: On September 4, 2023, a low-pressure system that would become Storm Daniel developed over southeastern Europe, initiating several days of exceptional precipitation and flooding in Greece.
reviews.source_dependence: NASA IMERG dates the genesis/development to September 4; ECMWF retrospective independently analyzes moisture sources and the prolonged September 4–7 Greek rainfall event. Both use satellite and ground-rainfall inputs but have distinct analysis methods.
reviews.unverified_cautions: September 4 was the low-pressure development and onset of multi-day rain, not the day on which all of Thessaly's extreme totals and flood impacts occurred. Libya's catastrophic flood occurred later and should not be folded into the September 4 Greece anniversary.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original September 4–7 storm track/IVT moisture source diagram and IMERG daily-rain sequence.

reviews.title_after: Flash flooding sweeps vehicles off Missouri low-water crossings
reviews.secondary_publisher: NWS Paducah and KFVS12 contemporaneous reporting
reviews.core_fact: On November 30, 2019, heavy rain caused dangerous flash flooding around Bollinger County, Missouri, sweeping vehicles off low-water crossings near Sedgewickville.
reviews.source_dependence: Original NCEI Sedgewickville flash-flood report and NWS Paducah's contemporaneous Storm Reports both use underlying local emergency-manager reports; KFVS12's independent on-scene fire/rescue interviews additionally corroborate date, location and impact.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Three fatalities occurred across separate low-water crossings, not all at one Sedgewickville bridge. Event report timestamps can be estimated and later casualty updates differ from preliminary storm reports; avoid exploitative or inaccurate casualty graphics.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original November 30 rainfall map and separate two low-water-crossing sites diagram.

reviews.title_before: Dense Fog — YOLO T W/NE SOLANO/SACRAMENTO T X SW/X W PLACER/X W AMADOR/S SUTTER, California
reviews.title_after: Freezing rain begins a crippling Northeast ice storm
reviews.location_after: Eastern New York and western New England, United States
reviews.core_fact: A major freezing-rain and sleet storm started December 11, 2008 across parts of New York and New England, causing extensive tree and power-line damage through December 12.
reviews.source_dependence: NWS Albany provides the dated precipitation type, soundings and event chronology; NASA Terra imagery independently documents the storm's regional aftermath but its outage count is from contemporary news reports.
reviews.unverified_cautions: This is a December 11–12 event; do not imply all ice accumulated December 11 or that NASA's post-storm December 13 image is a real-time scene. Regional outage counts are preliminary and have varying restoration dates.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original prefrontal warm-nose sounding, December 11–12 ice accretion swath and outage map.

reviews.title_after: Historic Meramec River flooding engulfs eastern Missouri
reviews.location_after: Pacific, Eureka and Meramec River communities, Missouri
reviews.core_fact: On December 29, 2015, eastern Missouri communities along the Meramec River were experiencing major flooding after prolonged late-December heavy rainfall.
reviews.source_dependence: MRCC's December 26–29 rainfall and Meramec impact summary and USGS December 29 flood documentation independently corroborate widespread Meramec basin flooding, while numerical river-gauge peaks trace to the same official hydrology network.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Record crests happened on different dates and streamgauges, some after December 29. St. Louis Mississippi River's notable crest occurred December 31; do not present it as a December 29 level. This is a flood anniversary, not the original December 29 New Orleans fog lead.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original Meramec River basin hydrographs keyed by station and exact crest dates.
